title: Analytic, holomorphic, and entire functions
terms: analytic function; holomorphic function; entire function; analytic rational function; higher complex derivatives; identity theorem; isolated zeros.

exposition.text:
A function is holomorphic on an open set when it is complex differentiable at every point of
that set. In complex analysis this is equivalent to being analytic, meaning locally represented
z
by a convergent power series. An entire function is holomorphic on all of C. Polynomials, e ,
sin z, and cos z are entire.
Rational functions are holomorphic away from denominator zeros, with cancellations possi-
bly producing removable singularities. Holomorphic functions have derivatives of every order,
and those derivatives are holomorphic. Differentiability on a line or at infinitely many isolated
points does not imply analyticity on any open set.
The identity theorem states that two holomorphic functions on a connected open domain are
identical if they agree at a set with an accumulation point inside that domain. Equivalently, a
nonzero holomorphic function has isolated zeros. An accumulation point only on the boundary
does not satisfy this hypothesis.

Let F be the entire extension of (z − 5z + 4)/(z − 1) across z = 1. What is F (1)?
(A) 0 (B) 5 (C) 10 (D) 20 (E) 120

solution.text:
5 2 3 4 5
Put h = z − 1. The numerator is (1 + h) − 5(1 + h) + 4 = 10h + 10h + 5h + h . After
2 3
division, the extension is 10 + 10h + 5h + h . Its second derivative at h = 0 is 2! · 5 = 10.
Cancellation produces a holomorphic extension with derivatives of every order.

question.text:
An entire function satisfies f (z)f (−z) = 0 for every z. Which conclusion follows?
(A) f is even and nonzero.
(B) f is identically zero.
(C) f is odd and nonzero.
(D) f has exactly one zero.
(E) f may be any polynomial with zero constant term.

solution.text:
If f(a) ̸= 0, continuity makes f nonzero on a neighborhood of a. The identity then forces
f(−z) = 0 throughout that neighborhood, so f vanishes on an open set and hence every-
where, a contradiction. Therefore no such a exists.
